# Deserialization that lets the data choose the types (C#)

`qualor:csharp/unsafe-deserialization` · Issue · Severity: High · [CWE-502](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/502.html) · OWASP Top 10: [A08:2025 Software or Data Integrity Failures](https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A08_2025-Software_or_Data_Integrity_Failures/), [A08:2021 Software and Data Integrity Failures](https://top10.owasp.org/2021/A08_2021-Software_and_Data_Integrity_Failures/)

## What it finds

<!-- begin: what-it-finds -->
Code that reads data with a .NET serializer that lets the data pick which types to create:

- `BinaryFormatter`, `SoapFormatter`, `NetDataContractSerializer`, `LosFormatter` and `ObjectStateFormatter`, reported where `Deserialize` (for `NetDataContractSerializer` also `ReadObject`) is called on a variable, field, parameter or new object of that type;
- Json.NET (Newtonsoft.Json) with `TypeNameHandling` set to `Auto`, `All`, `Objects` or `Arrays`: in a `JsonSerializerSettings` or `JsonSerializer`, on an MVC or Web API formatter's settings, or in a `[JsonProperty]`, `[JsonObject]`, `[JsonArray]` or `[JsonDictionary]` attribute (also `ItemTypeNameHandling`);
- `JavaScriptSerializer` created with a `SimpleTypeResolver`.

The rule looks at the API, whatever the data is; it does not need a request. `System.Text.Json`, `DataContractSerializer`, `XmlSerializer` and Json.NET with `TypeNameHandling.None` (the default) are not reported. Test code is skipped.
<!-- end: what-it-finds -->

## Why it matters

<!-- begin: why-it-matters -->
These serializers read type names from the payload and create objects of those types. An attacker who controls the bytes can name types already present in the application or the framework whose constructors, property setters or finalizers do something dangerous, and so run code in your process (remote code execution), read files or crash the service. Microsoft states that `BinaryFormatter` is never safe with untrusted input and cannot be made safe, and that its implementation was removed from the runtime in .NET 9 (it throws unless an unsupported compatibility package is installed). Data that looks trusted, such as a cookie, a queue message, a cache entry or a file a user can upload, often crosses a trust boundary without anyone noticing.
<!-- end: why-it-matters -->

## Example

<!-- begin: example -->
**Noncompliant:** the payload decides which types are created.

```csharp
using System.IO;
using Newtonsoft.Json;

public class MessageReader
{
    public object Read(string json)
    {
        var settings = new JsonSerializerSettings { TypeNameHandling = TypeNameHandling.Auto };
        return JsonConvert.DeserializeObject(json, settings);
    }
}
```

**Compliant:** a fixed type and no type names in the data.

```csharp
using System.IO;
using System.Text.Json;

public class MessageReader
{
    public Message Read(string json)
    {
        return JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Message>(json);
    }
}

public record Message(string Text);
```
<!-- end: example -->

## How to fix

<!-- begin: how-to-fix -->
- Read the data with a serializer bound to a fixed type: `System.Text.Json`, `DataContractSerializer` or `XmlSerializer`. Microsoft's migration guide for `BinaryFormatter` lists the options, including MessagePack and protobuf-net for binary data.
- With Json.NET leave `TypeNameHandling` at `None`. If you need polymorphic data, use `TypeNameHandling.Auto` only together with a `SerializationBinder` that allows an explicit list of types, or a custom converter that maps a discriminator field to known types.
- Never use `JavaScriptSerializer` with a `SimpleTypeResolver` or another type resolver on data you did not produce.
- If old `BinaryFormatter` payloads must still be read, use the safe reader for NRBF payloads described in Microsoft's migration guide, which does not create the types in the data.
<!-- end: how-to-fix -->

## Frameworks and APIs covered

- BinaryFormatter and other .NET formatters
- Json.NET (Newtonsoft.Json)
- JavaScriptSerializer (System.Web.Script.Serialization)

## Known limits

<!-- begin: known-limits -->
Under `qualor dotnet end`, Qualor's Roslyn engine checks this rule in OpenGrep's place, on the
projects the build compiled, with the compiler's types: a formatter is found by its type wherever
the object comes from (a helper's result, a field declared in another file), and it reads all C# the
compiler accepts. The engine's own limits are listed in the
[models' README](../../../models/README.md), sections "Misuse rules" and "Known limits". The bullets
below are the OpenGrep rule's: it runs outside `qualor dotnet end`, on C# files no compiled project
covers, and as the fallback when the engine cannot finish.

- OpenGrep finds a formatter when its type is written in the same file: a variable, field or parameter declared with it (also `var x = new BinaryFormatter()`), with or without a namespace. One returned by a helper, or kept in a member of another file, is missed.
- `TypeNameHandling` is reported where it is set to `Auto`, `All`, `Objects` or `Arrays` in the code. A value kept in a variable or constant is missed. A `SerializationBinder` that allows only expected types is not looked at: the setting is still reported. Settings used only to write JSON are reported too. The attribute form is matched as text, so it can also fire inside a comment or string.
- A `SimpleTypeResolver` kept in a variable before it is given to `JavaScriptSerializer`, and custom type resolvers, are missed.
- Code in a file OpenGrep cannot parse (some C# 11 and 12 syntax: `$$"""` raw strings, `class X : Y;`, some multi-line collection expressions) is not checked.
- Files under `test/`, `tests/`, `*.Tests/`, `*.UnitTests/`, `*.IntegrationTests/`, `*.Test/` and `*.Specs/` and named `*Tests.cs` or `*Test.cs` are skipped.
<!-- end: known-limits -->

## Tests

The test file [`rules/csharp/deserialization/unsafe-deserialization.cs`](../../../rules/csharp/deserialization/unsafe-deserialization.cs) holds every case the rule reports or accepts:
lines marked `ruleid:` must be reported and lines marked `ok:` must not. The known limits are
marked `todoruleid:` (missed) and `todook:` (wrongly reported). `npm test` runs them with OpenGrep,
and checks the example above as well.

The rule: [`rules/csharp/deserialization/unsafe-deserialization.yml`](../../../rules/csharp/deserialization/unsafe-deserialization.yml), added in version 2026.10.5.
